notes.reason: The claim is the author's own. Near the end he says in his own voice that "so far he has sent mixed signals on just how committed he is to building more at least market rate housing only focusing on publicly subsidized, permanently affordable, union built, rent stabilized homes", with no attribution to anyone else. It is worth knowing that this sentence is almost word for word from an Atlantic piece of 2 November 2025 about Mamdani's campaign platform, so the video, published on 4 August 2026, is repeating a judgement about the campaign as if it still described the sitting mayor. That is why the note has something real to say: Mamdani released his 112-page housing plan "Block by Block" in late May 2026, and independent write-ups of it (Cozen, Housing Wire, the city planning department itself) confirm the plan does pursue citywide transit-oriented development, neighbourhood rezonings in Brooklyn and the Bronx, higher residential density near transit and mixed-income housing on city-owned land, so the author's "only focusing on" is out of date and a viewer would come away with a wrong belief that matters to the video's closing argument about whether you can do both. What gives me pause is the note's first word of substance. It says the plan "explicitly includes market-rate housing production", and that is stronger than the evidence. The plan's own stated targets are 200,000 new affordable and 200,000 preserved affordable homes; there is no market-rate production target, and the note's own best source, The Real Deal of 16 June 2026, makes exactly the opposite point, that Mamdani's presentation "omitted that the plan relies on for-profit rental developments, which are about 70 percent market-rate". An author defending himself could fairly answer that a plan whose public messaging omits its reliance on market-rate building is the very definition of mixed signals. I could not open The Real Deal article directly (it answers 403), so I confirmed its headline, its deck about unleashing the private sector and the market-rate quote only through search snippets; the 70 percent share is plausible but the closest independent arithmetic I found, from Step Two Policy, implies a higher market-rate share. My recommendation is to send this only after rewording it to drop "explicitly" and to say plainly that the plan's own targets are affordable homes but that it pursues citywide upzoning and transit-oriented development and leans on cross-subsidy from largely market-rate buildings. Joeri Schasfoort is an economist whose whole video argues for building more, so a dated-fact correction that is friendly to his thesis is the kind he would plausibly take, but not in its current overstated form.
